power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Natural disasters, pandemics, armed conflict, and economic upheaval inflict lasting harm on mental wellbeing, yet what determines who recovers and who deteriorates remains poorly understood across crisis types.

Objectives: This review maps how crisis exposure shapes wellbeing across four crisis typologies, two surveillance modes (NLP-based and survey/administrative), and three impact directions (favorable, adverse, or mixed).

Eligibility criteria: Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers published in English between 2016 and 2026, applying machine learning, NLP, or deep learning methods to a population exposed to one of the four crisis typologies, and reporting at least one measurable mental health outcome.
PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore, supplemented by forward and backward citation searching and targeted keyword searches.
Factors were charted using the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health framework, adapted for the health system where the framework's coverage is thinnest.
They were sorted into tiers, subgroups, and subdimensions with maximum possible fidelity to the original framework.

Results: Across 338 code-able determinants, Intermediary Determinants, particularly psychosocial and behavioral-biological factors, accounted for two-thirds of coded determinants, while NLP-based methods proved most effective at capturing structural and contextual signals (e.g., governance, discoursebased constructs) rather than the clinical burden measures that dominate closer to the individual.
Favorable, protective constructs were both rarer and less computationally detected than adverse ones, concentrating almost entirely in mastery, self-concept, coping, and social capital.
Forty-five factors were set aside as Outcome Measures because they described prior symptoms, diagnoses, or the study's own outcome construct, with 8 being circular with the study's stated target.
Fewer studies examined economic downturns, and conflict studies had almost no NLP presence.
Conclusions: These findings demonstrate this field has matured methodologically in adverse detection but remains structurally limited in reach.

This is most evident in armed conflict contexts and in the surveillance of protective, resilience-oriented signals, highlighting the need for digital phenotyping, expanded NLP coverage, and wider adoption of explainable AI methods.
Mental health concerns have reached unprecedented levels, with more than one billion people living with one or more mental disorders (World Health Organization [WHO], 2025a).
Given a global count of 727,000 suicides each year among individuals aged 15 to 29 (WHO, 2025b), mental health problems have grown in prominence in the global health and development agenda.
text.formatted: Given a global count of 727,000 suicides each year among individuals aged 15 to 29 <ref type="bibr">(WHO, 2025b)</ref>, mental health problems have grown in prominence in the global health and development agenda.

text.text: Recent longitudinal research indicates that overlapping global crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine War, and economic recession result in functional impairments that persist long after these events resolve (Richter et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent longitudinal research indicates that overlapping global crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine War, and economic recession result in functional impairments that persist long after these events resolve <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Richter et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The cumulative psychological toll of recent epidemic crises, including SARS-CoV-1, Ebola, Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), and the Anthrax threat, has been studied (Esterwood & Saeed, 2020; Xiong et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The cumulative psychological toll of recent epidemic crises, including SARS-CoV-1, Ebola, Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), and the Anthrax threat, has been studied <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Esterwood & Saeed, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Xiong et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A review of crisis intervention strategies has also shown how intervention causes meaningful and significant improvements in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression outcomes (Hu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A review of crisis intervention strategies has also shown how intervention causes meaningful and significant improvements in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, understanding why some individuals are less resilient to crisis-induced psychological harm than others has driven a growing body of research in this field across diverse domains.
Yet, existing reviews of the factors causing crisis-induced psychological harm have been limited in scope.
They focus on single crisis types such as pandemics (Lieneck et al., 2021; Kunzler et al., 2021) and economic turmoil (Stein et al., 2023).
text.formatted: They focus on single crisis types such as pandemics <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Lieneck et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Kunzler et al., 2021)</ref> and economic turmoil <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Stein et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: They rely on survey-based and epidemiological primary studies, without integrating computational or data-driven methods, which have been shown to enable population-scale, real-time monitoring of mental health during crises (Tušl et al., 2022) and allow early detection of psychological distress signals before clinical presentation, supporting timely intervention during and after crisis events (Shatte et al., 2018).
text.formatted: They rely on survey-based and epidemiological primary studies, without integrating computational or data-driven methods, which have been shown to enable population-scale, real-time monitoring of mental health during crises <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Tušl et al., 2022)</ref> and allow early detection of psychological distress signals before clinical presentation, supporting timely intervention during and after crisis events <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Shatte et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: To address these gaps, this review treats wellbeing more comprehensively, examining predictive factors across four crisis typologies: natural disasters, pandemics and infectious disease outbreaks, armed conflict and forced displacement, and economic upheavals.
This paper adopts a scoping review methodology to systematically map the breadth of evidence across crisis types and wellbeing dimensions.

A scoping review is appropriate because the field is heterogeneous in methods, populations, and outcomes, and the aim is to map breadth and identify gaps rather than pool effect sizes (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005).
text.formatted: A scoping review is appropriate because the field is heterogeneous in methods, populations, and outcomes, and the aim is to map breadth and identify gaps rather than pool effect sizes <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arksey and O'Malley, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: A comparative analysis detailing how relevant wellbeing factors shift and differ across various crisis contexts and study modes.
An evaluation of computational explainability and ranking methods used to prioritize and order these factors when monitoring population-level wellbeing.
The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines the methodology used to identify, screen, and chart the included literature.
Section 3 introduces the foundational concepts of crisis exposure, mental wellbeing, and the identified taxonomy of factors across crisis contexts.
Section 4 presents these factors linking crisis exposure and mental wellbeing across four crisis typologies.
Section 5 contrasts the wellbeing outcomes of each crisis studied in this review.
Section 6 discusses conclusions, limitations, and future research directions and concludes the review.
This review followed PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al., 2018) and the Arksey and O'Malley (2005) framework as refined by Levac et al. (2010).
text.formatted: This review followed PRISMA-ScR <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Tricco et al., 2018)</ref> and the <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Arksey and O'Malley (2005)</ref> framework as refined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Levac et al. (2010)</ref>.

text.text: Using the PCC framework (Peters et al., 2022), this review targets adults and communities exposed to population-scale crises (military, civilian, healthcare worker, refugee, and disaster-survivor populations), aligned with WHO Mental Health Action Plan 2013 -2030 priorities (WHO, 2021).

text.text: Studies were eligible if they applied a machine learning, NLP, deep learning, or spatial modeling method with a predictive, classification, or clustering function; examined one of the four crisis typologies; and reported at least one mental health outcome.

We conducted a systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore on 27 June 2026, combining crisis, method, and outcome term blocks (2016-2026, English only), yielding 7,940 records (Supplement A).
Supplementary searching (citation chasing and keyword searches) identified 11 further records (forward citation n=3, backward citation n=3, keyword search n=5; Supplement B).
All results are archived in RIS/CSV on OSF.
The search strategy was structured around three core concepts: crisis exposure, mental health and wellbeing outcome, and computational method.
Crisis exposure terms included pandemic, natural disaster, armed conflict, refugee, and economic turmoil.
Mental health and wellbeing terms included PTSD, depression, anxiety, and resilience, as well as positive wellbeing terms such as flourishing and life satisfaction.
Computational method terms included machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and named algorithms such as random forest and support vector machines.

Terms within each concept were combined using OR and truncation, and the three concepts were combined using AND; a 2016 to 2026 date limit and English language filter were applied across all databases.
Full search strings for all four databases are provided in the Supplements.
Two reviewers conducted title/abstract and full-text screening independently, resolving disagreements through discussion or referral to a third reviewer.
Agreement at full-text screening was κ = 0.904 (6/133 disagreements).
Screening is summarized in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Screening is summarized in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Findings were synthesized narratively, grouped by crisis typology and analyzed across three areas: the wellbeing and non-wellbeing dimensions of outcomes and their associated factors (5.1), patterns of adverse, favorable, and mixed factors across crisis types (5.2), and computational methods and explainability (5.3).
Each factor was classified into named tiers, subgroups, and subdimensions adapted from the WHO CSDH framework (Table 1).
text.formatted: Each factor was classified into named tiers, subgroups, and subdimensions adapted from the WHO CSDH framework (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Given study heterogeneity, meta-analytic pooling was not possible; instead, each study's factors were tallied by direction, dimension, crisis typology, and computational method (NLP-based versus survey/administrative), so patterns could be compared within and across these groupings rather than pooled into a single effect size.

Studies reported factor prominence on two non-equivalent bases: outcome-linked (e.g., SHAP, permutation importance, regression coefficients), tied to a fitted model predicting a defined outcome and typically accompanied by a performance metric; and frequency-or association-based (e.g., topic/emotion frequency in NLP studies, association-rule support/confidence or causal-forest split weighting in survey studies), reflecting how often or strongly a theme or association appeared with no outcome variable modeled.
Findings are compared with two prior non-computational reviews in Section 5.3.
Data were extracted using a standardized charting form, piloted on five included studies.

Charted variables included bibliographic information, crisis typology, country/setting, study design, data source type, sample size, computational method(s), evidence type (prediction-focused vs. pattern-focused, following Tu et al., 2025), primary outcome(s), and predictive factor classification.

Background

This review adopts the conceptual framework for action on the social determinants of health developed by Solar & Irwin (2010) for the World Health Organization Commission on Social Determinants of Health.
text.formatted: This review adopts the conceptual framework for action on the social determinants of health developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Solar & Irwin (2010)</ref> for the World Health Organization Commission on Social Determinants of Health.

text.text: It organizes health inequities along a causal chain moving from socioeconomic and political context through structural determinants to intermediary determinants of health.

The framework has since been applied and extended in later work, including a systematic review of disaster health literature (Nomura et al., 2016) and a recent refinement of the original World Health Organization structure using empirical case material (Karatekin et al., 2024 (Karatekin et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: The framework has since been applied and extended in later work, including a systematic review of disaster health literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Nomura et al., 2016)</ref> and a recent refinement of the original World Health Organization structure using empirical case material <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Karatekin et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Karatekin et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: The framework organizes crisis determinants into three causal tiers: (1) Structural Determinants (governance, policy, social position) generate a person's socioeconomic position and socio-political context, which determine differential exposure to risk, differential vulnerability once exposed, and differential consequences of illness; (2) Bridging Determinants (social cohesion and social capital) carry that structural position down to the individual, or fail to; and (3) Intermediary Determinants (material, psychosocial, behavioral, health-system) convert this into the lived health outcome.
CSDH fixes the direction of this pipeline and the four intermediary categories, but leaves open how each subdimension is operationalized, and how finely subdimensions are split.
The present taxonomy proposed in the paper follows the textual authority of Solar & Irwin to guide classification.
text.formatted: The present taxonomy proposed in the paper follows the textual authority of Solar & Irwin to guide classification.

text.text: Every subdimension corresponding to a construct named in the source text, whether stated without qualification or introduced through a hedged example list, was retained faithfully and traced to its originating passage.

This procedure follows directed content analysis (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005) and the deductive qualitative content analysis process described by Elo & Kyngäs (2008), in which theory-derived categories are applied to a corpus as predetermined codes .

text.text: Governance, as coded here, consolidates state action across three registers: direct governance and restriction measures, macroeconomic policy, and public policy content.

These are combined into a single subdimension because crisis literature items along macroeconomic and public policy lines were too sparse individually to support their own subdimensions and share a common state action character with governance content proper.
Epidemiological Conditions has been modified to track the same information for all types of crises, not just epidemics as it did originally.

Renamed Contextual and Environmental Conditions, it tracks the crisis's objective, measurable scale, case counts, environmental hazard severity, and so on, distinct from the state's political response.
Solar & Irwin acknowledge directly that a full characterization of the socioeconomic and political context was beyond the scope of their paper.

text.text: An earlier draft of the framework had attempted to include every element in a single diagram, and the authors report that this approach was abandoned as unhelpful.
The need for extension is greatest precisely where the source framework's own coverage is thinnest.

The health system discussion, although substantive on financing and equitable access, never engages with psychiatric care, psychological support, or mental health service delivery at any point in the document.
This asymmetry follows directly from the framework's origins in socioeconomic epidemiology and intersectoral policy rather than clinical or psychological science.
This review has followed the CSDH framework with maximum fidelity, taking most of its constructs verbatim.

Because the framework provides an overarching structure whose subdimension content is illustrative rather than exhaustive, applying it to a review of crisis literature necessarily surfaces content the source framework does not itself name.
This is an expected consequence of applying a general health equity policy framework outside the context of its original construction (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005).

text.text: This review anchors the psychosocial determinants in Pearlin's Stress Process Model (Pearlin et al., 1981) because it provides an empirically validated account of how discrete Life Events and Chronic Strains erode self-concept and elevate psychological distress, mediated by the individual's Coping mechanisms and ideals of Mastery and Self Concept.

text.text: CSDH's own text supplies anchors for four of Pearlin's five roles in one passage.

It is defined as "psychosocial stressors (for example, negative life events and job strain), stressful living circumstances (e.g., high debt) and (lack of) social support, coping styles, etc.", which covers discrete events and job strain as Life Events, ongoing debt as Chronic Strains, and coping directly.

CSDH also anticipates Mastery and Self Concept and Personality Traits, describing how "people perceive the events related to their health as controllable (internal control) or as controlled by others (external control)".
CSDH anchors the Behavioral and Biological subdimension firmly to the body and to conduct, never to relational or cognitive experience.
Its definition is entirely physical: smoking, diet, alcohol consumption, and lack of physical exercise, with genetic factors folded in among the biological factors.
Nothing in this definition touches relationships or cognition, just as nothing in the Psychosocial definition touches physiology.
That asymmetry marks the boundary between the two subdimensions: one is oriented to the person's perceived and relational environment; the other to the person's physiology and conduct.

text.text: This section maps the 70 included studies by crisis type, population, computational method, analytical basis, and reported key finding.
Associated factors that significantly contribute to mental wellbeing outcomes following crisis exposure can be split into three types: favorable, mixed, and adverse factors.
Adverse factors increase the probability of wellbeing deterioration, while favorable factors buffer against it.
Mixed or non-monotonic factors may increase the probability in some situations and decrease it in others.
Of the 23 studies in this category, 11 use NLP or text-based methods (Table 2) and 13 use survey or administrative data (Table 3).

text.text: Method choice tracks data type: text-based studies predominantly use transformer architectures (BERT, RoBERTa, or fine-tuned variants) for emotion and sentiment classification, while survey-based studies predominantly use tree-based ensembles (random forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost) to rank candidate variables.

Populations range from general social media users (Ou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2023) to specific subgroups such as healthcare workers (Zhou et al., 2022; Elyashar et al., 2021), pregnant women (Nichols et al., 2022; Dhankar & Katz, 2023), and older adults (Xiang et al., 2025).

text.text: Table 10 displays every CSDH tier down to subdimension level, with direction of effect and the actual terms each subdimension draws on.
Across the three tiers, 338 factors were code-able: 81 under Structural Determinants, 33 under Bridging Determinants, and 224 under Intermediary Determinants.
A further 45 factors are categorized under the Outcome Measures tier because they measure symptoms, prior diagnoses, or the study's own outcome instrument rather than its determinants.
Another 5 factors remain Not Coded (Excluded/Uncategorizable).
At the tier level, Structural Determinants accounted for 81 of the 338 code-able determinant factors.
It sits furthest upstream, defined as the socioeconomic and political conditions of a society that decide who is exposed to a crisis and who has resources to withstand it.
This tier splits into two subgroups: Socioeconomic Position and Socioeconomic and Political Context.

This refers to an individual's economic and social standing within society, captured through markers such as occupation, age, income, education, gender, and race or ethnicity.
Occupation was consistently adverse (e.g., forced retirement, unstable employment, work disruption), revealing that job loss and disruption are detrimental to mental health outcomes across contexts.

NLP methods also identified related factors in media discourse and news coverage about loss and unemployment, unlike structural markers such as age and gender, which were rarely discussed in this way.
It appeared more heavily across pandemic and financial crises (n = 10 combined), showing how both public health restrictions and economic contraction independently cause job losses.
Age was the second-largest subdimension (n = 10), coded as adverse or favorable depending on the age range.
It appeared evenly across all four crisis types and was collected fully through non-NLP demographic fields in surveys rather than through text.
Age is not typically self-reported in media discourse the way sentiment or symptom language is.
Similarly, Gender was coded as adverse overall, though no consistent direction by gender emerged from this review.
Male and female categories were both adverse or favorable depending on context.
Like Age, it was captured entirely through non-NLP demographic intake fields.
Education was predominantly protective (e.g., educational attainment, functional literacy, language skills).

It was almost absent from pandemic and financial crisis studies, suggesting that educational attainment was more likely to be investigated in displacement and conflict cohort studies to be profiled against standard baseline demographics.
Non-NLP methods, for the same reason as Age and Gender, mainly collected it.
Race and Ethnicity and Income remained too small to analyze.
However, Financial Means under the Material Circumstances subgroup also captured the same signals as Income.

Financial Means (n = 15, e.g., financial worries, income insecurity, asset loss), which is under the Intermediary Tier and the Material Circumstances subgroup but is being discussed here, was almost entirely adverse and appeared across all four crisis types in a fairly even distribution.
This shows the universal relevance and impact of economic hardship regardless of any crisis context.
It was mineable from news coverage of price surges, shortages, and economic shocks.
This refers to the governance, policy, and environmental conditions surrounding a person, rather than anything about the individual directly.
Governance (n = 12, e.g., government stringency measures, lockdown, misinformation & criticism) was coded as adverse, as it was more often treated as a source of distress than support.

text.text: It was concentrated in pandemic and natural disaster research (n = 11 combined), where it plays an active intervening role.
NLP detected it in 10 of 12 instances, since lockdown orders and government reactions are directly reported in media and social media text.

Contextual and Environmental Conditions (n = 16) skewed adverse (e.g., number of cases, deaths, severe weather and natural hazards), as case counts, death tolls, and hazard severity are likely to elicit negative mental impacts.
This appeared only in pandemic (n = 6) and natural disaster research (n = 10), the two crisis types in which an objective, publicly reported magnitude of the event itself is routinely tracked.

They were NLP-dependent, with 11 of 16 instances found by NLP, since case counts and hazard figures appear in both mined news text and structured records such as epidemiological or meteorological data.
Culture and Societal Values (n = 7) showed a mixed valence, split across pandemic and armed conflict research, and was well detected by NLP.
Armed conflict research also shows a gap that the other three crisis types do not share.
It has zero coverage of Governance or Contextual and Environmental Conditions, meaning the political context around conflict has not been studied at all.
Bridging Determinants (n = 33, 16 Adv, 13 Fav, 4 Mix).
At the tier level, Bridging Determinants accounted for 33 of the 338 code-able factors, with 16 coded as adverse.
It was the most evenly balanced tier in the taxonomy, as shown in Table 11.

text.text: Bridging Determinants sit in the middle of the CSDH tier structure and refer to factors that either carry the protection of a favorable structural position down to the individual or fail to do so.
This tier contains a single subgroup, Social Cohesion and Social Capital.

Bridging Determinants correspond to the Cross-Cutting tier in the coded dataset.
This refers to the family, community, and institutional ties available to a person during a crisis, and is the most evenly balanced subgroup in the taxonomy.
Bonding Social Capital (n = 18, e.g., friend/family/peer support, family support, parental involvement) shows this balance: protective ties with close kin buffer against negative outcomes.
At the same time, adverse markers such as loss of relatives or living alone are associated with worse outcomes.
It was beneficial across all crises, since close kin are affected by the same shocks and can often help each other at the same time.
Bridging Social Capital (n = 15, e.g., supportive online communities, social network, social inclusion) shows the same balance.
Protective community ties buffer against adverse outcomes across crises, whilst absence, exclusion, or isolation causes negative outcomes.
Both were captured through NLP and non-NLP methods alike: family and community relationship discussions can also be found in social media discourse.

Intermediary Determinants sit closest to the individual and the outcome itself, referring to material circumstances, psychosocial stressors and coping, health behaviors and biology, and contact with the health system through which a crisis becomes lived distress or lived resilience.

text.text: Life Events (Acute/Discrete) was the largest subdimension (n = 42, e.g., total trauma load, previous trauma, adverse childhood experiences) and was almost entirely adverse, concentrated in armed conflict research (n = 27).

The reason for both adversity and concentration is that discrete traumatic exposure, such as combat, displacement, and sexual violence, is a defining feature in conflict and displacement cohort studies.
Life events were captured mostly through non-NLP structured trauma checklists (32 of 42), which can only be collected clinically rather than by mining media text.
Both non-NLP and NLP methods have detected coping mechanisms.

Coping mechanisms received the most concentrated attention in pandemic studies, suggesting researchers have explored the psychological impacts of beneficial and adverse coping less thoroughly in other crisis types.
Coping is nearly evenly split (11 Adv, 10 Fav) as coping strategies can be coded in either direction depending on whether the strategy itself is adaptive or maladaptive.

Mastery and Self Concept was also a favorable subdimension (n = 29, e.g., resilience, coping self-efficacy, sense of coherence), concentrated in pandemic (n = 11) and armed conflict (n = 10) research.
Like coping, it was extracted from sentiment-based proxies for resilience and optimism in mined discourse (n = 8).
It was a majority-favorable subdimension (15 Fav of 29).
Resilience and coping self-efficacy are, by construction, framed as protective resources rather than harms.
Personality Traits (n = 10, e.g., emotional stability, self-control, optimism, extraversion) was a subdimension in which favorable codes outnumber adverse ones (1 Adv, 4 Fav, 5 Mix).
This could also be because protective traits such as optimism and self-control are more common than harmful traits.
It was concentrated in natural disaster (n = 6) and pandemic (n = 4) research and was captured entirely through non-NLP methods.

Chronic Strains due to ambient threat or uncertainty (n = 32, e.g., fear of coronavirus, uncertainty about pandemic development, worry about infection) were concentrated in pandemic research (n = 17), with a smaller presence in others.
Uncertainty or risk of an unresolved threat of infection or aftershock is a more central experience in pandemics than in others; thus, it was ranked as adverse ( 29Adv).

text.text: In contrast, it leaned toward non-NLP methods (11 of 32 NLP, 34%), since fear and threat language is expressed as readily in mined text as in survey responses.
This refers to the lifestyle choices and physiological traits through which structural social inequities directly translate into individual health outcomes.
All subdimensions are almost entirely coded as adverse, and almost no item is coded as favorable.

This total absence of favorable coding across the subgroup follows directly from how these constructs are defined: a burden, an illness, or a biomarker abnormality has little room to be recorded as a positive outcome in the first place.

Moreover, they are captured almost entirely through non-NLP methods (21 of 25, 84%), since self-rated health and diagnosed conditions are typically collected as clinical or survey items rather than mined from open text.
Cumulative Physiological Burden (n = 25, e.g., self-rated health, hypertension, cancer) was predominantly adverse (17 of 25).
It was concentrated in armed conflict research (n = 11) and pandemic research (n = 12).

Health Behaviors (n = 12, e.g., smoking, recent testing, sedentary lifestyle, time outdoors, Mediterranean diet adherence) were concentrated in pandemic research (n = 7) and were adverse in 9 of 12 items.
This was because maladaptive and health risk behaviors were tracked as a consequence of crisis stress.
Some of its discourse surfaced in mined social media text (e.g., leisure-or substance-related language), similar to psychosocial circumstances.
Direct Biomarker Panel (n = 11, e.g., BMI, white-matter tract markers, blood-based biomarkers) was captured in only 2 studies exploring the biomarker predictors of mental health.
This refers to a person's financial resources and housing conditions during a crisis.
Financial Means has been discussed with Income above under Income within the Socioeconomic Position subgroup and Structural Determinants tier.
Housing (n = 14, e.g., property loss, relocation, permanent displacement) was equally uniformly adverse.
It was almost fully confined to natural disaster research (n = 12, 86%).
This is because housing loss is a defining physical consequence of disasters and conflicts, but in a public health restriction or an economic contraction, the home itself typically remains intact.
Both Financial Means and Housing were found in media discourse and survey instruments.
The material work environment i.e., Material Work Environment subdimension (e.g., housework, working from home, schooling from home) was too small to judge.
This refers to a person's contact with, and receipt of support from, formal health and psychosocial services during a crisis.
It is the only intermediary category in which favorable codes outnumber adverse ones.
Access is split evenly (4 Adv, 4 Fav), capturing both the presence and absence of healthcare as substantively meaningful outcomes.
Access (n = 8, e.g., medical needs past 30 days, distance to pediatric ICU, distance to alcohol/drug treatment center) appeared only in natural disasters (n = 3) and armed conflict (n = 5) research.
It was captured entirely administrative surveys and clinical methods.
Responsiveness and System Performance (n=1, e.g., receiving psychological support material) had too few observances to discuss further.
Outcome Measures (n = 45, 44 Adv, 0 Fav, 1 Mix).
These items sit outside the three CSDH determinant tiers because they describe prior diagnoses, current symptoms, or the study's own outcome construct rather than a cause of wellbeing.
They represent the study's output rather than factors leading to it.
These items are often symptoms or related outcomes of the very distress or disorder that the study is designed to predict.
Eight of these outcomes are circular with the study's own target.
The analytical basis linking factors to outcomes was recorded for all 69 studies.

Non-NLP studies overwhelmingly fit a formal statistical or machine learning ranking: 50 of 51 non-NLP studies use SHAP, feature or variable importance, regression or LASSO coefficients, or a comparable technique, and only one study (Li et al., 2024) reports no ranking basis at all but only has 6 factors.

text.text: NLP studies show a pattern close to the opposite.

Of the 17 NLP studies with a recorded basis, only 5 report a formal statistical measure, limited to correlation (Ou, de Bruijn & Schulz, 2025) or regression and path coefficients (Wu et al., 2023; Bathina et al., 2021; Elyashar et al., 2021; Karami et al., 2026), and none use SHAP, permutation importance, or any tree-based importance measure.

text.text: Other NLP studies mostly characterize factors through purely descriptive frequency measures, operationalizing importance almost entirely as how often a topic or sentiment appears in the text rather than how strongly it predicts an outcome.
Comparison with previous studies Schäfer et al.
(2024), Kunzler et al. (2021), and Newnham et al. ( 2022) remain the most relevant prior reviews of crisis mental health, each methodologically sound within its own remit.

text.text: None includes a computational or machine learning method as an inclusion criterion, and this difference in scope produces a difference in what each review can structurally find.
Schäfer et al. restricts to regression models in highincome countries; Kunzler et al. restricts to early pandemic survey data; Newnham et al. explicitly excludes conflict-and violence-related trauma.

This review's machine learning and NLP inclusion criterion is what surfaces actually impacted populations such as refugees, disaster-exposed civilians, Ugandan and Sri Lankan war survivors, and constructs that regression-based synthesis in high-income cohorts is not designed to reach.
Moreover, this review coded factors under the CSDH framework, extended by stress process models, to build the organizing taxonomy.
This produced 338 determinants sorted into Structural, Bridging, and Intermediary tiers across 24 subdimensions, a resolution none of the three prior reviews approach.
Every coded item was then cross-tabulated by crisis typology and by detection modality (NLP vs. non-NLP).
This double stratification showed where the burden is concentrated by crisis type and how invisible that burden is to computational detection.
On age, it proves consistently unstable rather than resolving to one direction.
Education diverges between the two prior reviews (Kunzler protective vs.
Schäfer largely null), and the present review leans closer to Kunzler, with a favorable tilt.
Emotion regulation/psychological flexibility, favorable in Schäfer et al., becomes far more heterogeneous in the present review's 29-item Mastery and Self Concept subdimension.

Governance, Occupation, Financial Circumstances, Housing, and the biological/behavioral subdimensions were untested by all three prior reviews because each was restricted by a different eligibility axis (high-income countries, early pandemic data, or non-conflict disaster/pandemic exposure), and none stratified by detection method.
>Synthesis, Future Directions, and Limitations
text.formatted: <head n="6." >Synthesis, Future Directions, and Limitations</head>

text.text: Across the evidence base, 338 code-able determinants were charted using the WHO CSDH, with Intermediary Determinants (psychosocial circumstances and behavioral and biological factors chief among them) accounting for 66.3% of the total.
In contrast, Structural and Bridging Determinants together account for just over a third.

Armed conflict is captured almost entirely through structured clinical instruments rather than textbased methods, unlike pandemic and natural disaster research, which has more instances of NLP detection.
Armed conflict research also shows zero coverage of governance or environmental conditions, leaving the effects of political context on trauma in conflict settings unexamined.
Prior trauma and pre-existing psychiatric burden are the most consistent predictors of later distress, more so than any feature of the conflict exposure itself.
This suggests that harm accumulates on prior vulnerability rather than arising fresh from a single event.
In pandemics, the dominant psychosocial pattern is prolonged, unresolved uncertainty rather than a discrete shock.

Coping and resilience constructs are also studied far more heavily here than in any other crisis type, giving pandemic research the most developed evidence base in the review for protective psychosocial mechanisms.

In economic upheavals, occupational and income disruption is adverse almost without exception across the available studies, showing how economic disruption itself is the central pathogenic factor in this crisis type.
This crisis type is also the least evidenced in the review, with only five studies across both NLP and survey methods combined.
Natural disasters show that harm extends well beyond the disaster event itself, driven mainly by prolonged material and residential disruption such as property loss, displacement, and relocation.
NLP-based methods capture governance and contextual signals well, with 10 of 12 governance items and over half of contextual items derived from mined text.
Structural Determinants carry the highest NLP rate of any tier.
The tiers closest to the individual are captured almost entirely through non-NLP clinical or survey instruments.
Categories drawn from discourse, such as governance and ethnicity, are NLP-heavy, while every demographic, biomarker, clinical, and administrative factor is drawn from non-NLP sources.
Fifty of 51 non-NLP studies apply a formal statistical or machine learning ranking to justify their factors.
Eleven of 17 NLP studies base their justification on descriptive frequency counts.
Rather than fitting formal rankings, these NLP studies mostly operationalize importance as how often a topic or sentiment appears in the text.
Only 9 studies overall use SHAP (Table 14), so this field requires wider adoption of explainable AI techniques for more interpretable results.
text.formatted: Only 9 studies overall use SHAP (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_7">14</ref>), so this field requires wider adoption of explainable AI techniques for more interpretable results.

text.text: Adverseness dominates 6 of the taxonomy's subdimensions at 85% or higher.
It spans life events, chronic strains, financial means, housing, material work environment, and direct biomarker panel.
Favorable signal concentrates almost entirely in mastery, self-concept, and coping constructs, together accounting for 25 of the corpus's 72 favorable codes.
Six subdimensions, including Life Events, Chronic Strains, and Housing, show zero favorable coding across all methods.
Prior symptoms, diagnoses, and the study's own outcome construct sit outside the three determinant tiers; eight of these are circular with the study's own stated target.
Computational methods and NLP approaches should be expanded specifically into the crisis types and constructs where they remain structurally absent.
They also need to detect protective, not only adverse, constructs.
Researchers at the intersection of AI, business, and social economics need to study economic downturns more.

Armed conflict is captured almost entirely through structured clinical instruments rather than text-based methods, in contrast to the subdimensions where NLP already dominates in pandemic and natural disaster research.
Armed conflict research also shows zero coverage of governance or environmental conditions, leaving the effects of political context on trauma in conflict settings unexamined.

Digital phenotyping should be used more widely across all crisis types, as its value for tracking behavioral and mental health signals is well established in the clinical literature (Onnela & Rauch, 2016).
text.formatted: Digital phenotyping should be used more widely across all crisis types, as its value for tracking behavioral and mental health signals is well established in the clinical literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Onnela & Rauch, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This involves collecting passive data from phones and wearables, such as movement, screen time, sleep, and typing behavior.

This would allow chronic strain and health behavior to be tracked continuously without repeated surveys, which is especially useful in conflict zones or disaster areas where survey access is often limited.
The broader contextual and semantic range of large language models (LLMs) makes them more capable of picking up the subtler, less standardized language of mastery, self-concept, and coping.

GPT-based models, for example, have already been shown to detect psychological constructs from text more accurately than traditional dictionary-based methods across multiple languages (Rathje et al., 2024).

text.text: These gaps point toward constructing a knowledge graph that integrates evidence across the CSDH tiers into a unified computational structure, and toward bringing formal explainable AI methods more broadly into crisis mental health research.

A graph linking structural determinant data, bridging determinant data, and intermediary outcome data would allow new crisis events to be mapped onto the existing evidence base, identifying at-risk populations and intervention priorities across tiers rather than within a single subgroup in isolation.

Moreover, regardless of whether the underlying model is NLP-based, adopting purpose-built explanation methods such as SHAP, LIME, or causal machine learning (rather than relying on frequency counts or a model's native feature importance as a stand-in) would raise the evidentiary standard across the field.
This review has four main limitations.

First, consistent with PRISMA-ScR guidance for scoping reviews, we did not conduct a formal quality or risk-of-bias appraisal, since the review's purpose was to map the breadth of the evidence rather than weight it.
As a result, this synthesis represents methodologically stronger and weaker studies on equal footing.

Second, our characterization of certain factors as the "strongest" predictors reflects how consistently they rank highly across studies, not a pooled effect size: importance scores and odds ratios are not directly comparable across different methods and study designs.
This vote-counting approach is standard for scoping reviews and well suited to mapping breadth, but it cannot quantify any single factor's contribution relative to others.
Third, the literature coverage is not exhaustive.
The search was supplemented by forward and backward citation searching, consistent with recommended scoping review practice (Levac et al., 2010).

text.text: Still, some relevant studies may have been missed, particularly those published in non-English venues or in regional computer science conference proceedings not indexed in the four databases searched.
Fourth, and most consequentially, this evidence base relies heavily on social media data.

Across all four crisis types, included studies drew predominantly on Twitter, Reddit, Weibo, and YouTube, which capture people with internet access and digital literacy rather than the populations a crisis affects most severely, such as older generations or lower-income groups.
These biases compound with population gaps that differ by crisis type.
Across all four crisis types, low-and middle-income countries are underrepresented relative to high-income contexts.

This scoping review mapped 70 studies applying machine learning, NLP, deep learning, and spatial modeling methods to mental health and resilience outcomes across four population-scale crisis types: pandemics, economic upheavals, natural disasters, and armed conflict or displacement.

Current computational systems largely detect distress only once it has produced a structured clinical record, rarely extending to the governance, contextual, and coping constructs this review finds carry the most computationally accessible signal upstream of that record.
Crisis mental health research has matured methodologically but not yet diversified in what it measures or whom it reaches.

Closing the burden visibility gap, linking structural and contextual signals to individual-level clinical outcomes, expanding the evidence on economic upheavals, extending NLP into armed conflict contexts, and detecting more protective constructs represent the clearest paths toward more equitable computational crisis mental health surveillance.
